newsitem.title: JAPAN: American freed by N.Korea paid hotel bill, no fine.
newsitem.headline: American freed by N.Korea paid hotel bill, no fine.

text.p: A young American detained in North Korea for three months as a spy flew to freedom on Wednesday after paying a hotel bill of about $5,000 but no fine, the congressman who negotiated his release said.

A weary-looking Carl Hunziker raised his arms in a victory salute when he stepped from a U.S. Air Force C-21 plane that flew him from the North Korean capital of Pyongyang to this U.S. air base on the outskirts of Tokyo.

Congressman Bill Richardson, a close confidant of President Bill Clinton, who went to North Korea to negotiate the release, said his trip not only freed Hunziker but gave him renewed hope that Pyongyang was ready again to work at decreasing tension on the Korean Peninsula.
"He (Hunziker) said he was treated in a humanitarian fashion by the North Koreans," Richardson told reporters.
After undergoing medical tests, Hunziker, who did not give a news conference, was scheduled to fly to the United States later in the day to be home in time for Thanksgiving Day.

Richardson, who in 1994 negotiated the release of a U.S. Air Force helicopter pilot shot down when he strayed into North Korean air space near the border with South Korea, said nothing was given by the United States in return for Hunziker's release.
Asked about demands that Hunziker should pay for time he spent in a hotel while his case was decided, Richardson said:

"On that amount, what we paid was a small amount, no more than $5,000. North Korean judicial authorities imposed a fine for illegal entry into their country but that fine was not paid. There was no quid pro quo by the United States."
Hunziker, 26, who his family says is a missionary, was detained by North Korea near the border with China on August 24 when he crossed the Yalu River separating the two countries.
He was held on charges of espionage and illegal entry.
The United States, South Korea and Hunziker's family have all denied he is a spy and say he accidentally strayed into North Korea while on a visit to China.
"He made a mistake... He's not a spy," Richardson told reporters.
Dozens of journalists were on hand for Richardson and Hunziker's arrival in rain at about 12.30 p.m. (0330 GMT)
Richardson and Hunziker had been scheduled to leave North Korea for Tokyo on Tuesday. But their departure was delayed for a day for reasons which were not yet known.
The two men, both smiling widely, clasped hands and raised their arms above their heads as U.S. military personnel applauded.
Hunziker, from Parkland, Washington, walked unaided to a waiting car which whisked him off to the base's hospital. He was dressed in sweat pants and a military-style parka.
"He's a very religious young man and he was emotional about returning home. I think he's very firm in his beliefs," Richardson said.

The congressman said that in talks with North Korean officials he gained the impression that Pyongyang wanted to put behind it a recent incident involving one of its submarines which South Korea says was on an infiltration mission.
"My sense is that the North Korean government wants to get the submarine incident behind it and re-engage with the international community," Richardson said
